Electromagnetic radiation: People need to work on their bullshit detection

TL~DW of the video: Guy takes an "Electromagnetic radiation detector" and puts it up to a compact fluorescent bulb. Surprise, surprise, he detects radiation. And anything that's radiation is bad right?

What is electromagnetic radiation?

Electromagnetic radiation is a magnetic and electric field perpendicular to each other that travel together. It is one way that energy moves about. Visible light is the form of electromagnetic radiation that people are most familiar with. That's right, every time you see something, that's your eye absorbing some of this super scary radiation stuff. In fact, everything with a temperature higher than 0 K (absolute zero) emits at least some amount of electromagnetic radiation. Even you emit thermal radiation. That's what those infrared cameras pick up. That's also how ovens cook your food. The elements are energized, and that energy radiates out and cooks your food.

Just because the man in the video is picking up something called radiation then, doesn't mean he's detecting anything dangerous, and it doesn't mean you have to throw out your compact fluorescent bulbs. (But you should consider replacing them with more efficient LEDs.)

Why is "radiation" so scary?

Electromagnetic radiation exists on a spectrum. You can see the visible light portion of the spectrum is relatively small. Anything to the right of that (smaller frequency, longer wavelength) is generally pretty safe. There's the infrared lights that keep your pet lizards warm, FM radio to carry your favorite tunes, and other useful frequencies.

To the left though, lies serious danger Electromagnetic radiation increases in energy as the frequency increases. Ultraviolet light that's absorbed by cells will damage and degrade the cells. This is how you get sunburns and most types of skin cancer. Damage to the Ozone layer is such a huge deal because it protects us from the sun's UV radiation. Probably one of the reasons why Mars appears to be so lifeless is that there's no protective Ozone layer. Any biological (as we know it) material would be quickly destroyed on the surface of Mars from UV light. (That's not to say there's no life hiding from the light under the surface.)

Higher and higher energies and frequencies cause more damage when they are absorbed. You wear lead vests when you get an X-ray because of just how much damage even a limited dose can do (don't be afraid of them though, the dose is still very small.) Gamma rays above that are truly devastating. People on the K-19 died in just weeks after exposure to high levels of gamma radiation. The sun puts out quite a bit of gamma rays, but the Earth's magnetic fields protect us, and channel the rays to the north and south poles to create the Aurora. Mars doesn't have much of a magnetic field, so any biologic material on it is very unprotected. The other chief reason why it appears to be so lifeless.

What in the heck is that guy detecting then?

Apparently not much if the reviews are to be believed. Pause the video when he shows the face of the detector he's using, and you'll see it's the thing I just linked. The specifications say it detects radiation in the range of 50Hz to 2000Hz. Looking at our handy electromagnetic specturm from above, that's all well in the range of long radio waves. Certainly not anything dangerous.

Sanity Check

Electromagnetic radiation emissions are very tightly controlled by governments across the globe. They need to know that you switching on your microwave oven won't interfere with airplanes, emergency radios, cell phones, WiFi, pacemakers military communications, and so on. They also don't want you clogging up their (private or public) health care systems with fifteen different types of cancer by the time you're twelve. Virtually everything that might possibly emit electromagnetic radiation is tested by agencies around the world to make sure that they're safe for you and the country to use.

Because it's so much easier to watch a video, get scared, and re-post than it is to educate, or get educated about what's really going on.
